what_it_does: Before a chip can be manufactured, engineers must verify that electrical signals will arrive at every destination on time — a process called static timing analysis (STA). There are two main ways to do this: a fast but pessimistic method (graph-based analysis, or GBA) that may declare a chip too slow when it is actually fine, and a slow but accurate method (path-based analysis, or PBA) that checks every signal route individually. At modern, nanometer-scale manufacturing nodes, even the fast method produces results that can differ meaningfully from a full transistor-level simulation (called SPICE), making sign-off — the final green-light before tape-out — less reliable. GTN-Path is a machine-learning system based on graph transformer networks (a type of neural network that reasons over graph-structured data using attention, a mechanism that lets the model weigh which neighbors matter most) that learns to predict how a signal waveform evolves as it travels through logic gates and wires. By mimicking the physical propagation of signals as a learned process, it achieves about 3% error relative to full SPICE simulations while running over 3,500 times faster.
